chapter: Faith, Paris life and later years
title: Teaching at the Conservatoire Saint-Germain and its dropping of jazz
summary: He taught five years at a municipal conservatory, growing it from four to 89 students, until the director dropped jazz hoping for national status and then asked him back.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: : Yeah. Listen, Kenny, the one last thing I didn't ask you was -- I really haven't brought you right up to date. So what is life like now? Like you said that you were teaching, that you are teaching, Teddy Wilson's boy.
: That lives here. And I guess you do quite a lot of teaching, don't you?
Yes, I do. I taught at the Conservatoire Saint Germain-Orleans.
Five years I was out there.

Uh-huh. And then I opened -- we opened our own school and all that. But it's things -- you know, what happened at the Conservatoire Saint Germain-Orleans was a funny thing. Which they were going to be nationalized, which meant that the state was going to pay for everything.
Yeah, I see what you mean.
So when a conservatory 's national, that's a big thing.
You know, like the Conservatoire National, the Musique Superieure, and all that, you know.
Because we don't have many national conservatories in France.

So by St. Germaine being such a rich municipality, they were going to make it a national conservatory. So what does the director do, after being -- I was there five years, and he was saying, "Oh, Kenny, your work is so beautiful. I love you." If you could see the letter he wrote me after all that. Then they decided they were going to get rid of jazz or they wouldn't be made national. So they scratched jazz off, and he wrote me a letter. He says listen, I'm sorry, but we have to drop your program, and blah, blah, blah. So I said okay. It's okay with me, Mr. Pirot Billet (PHONETIC). It doesn't matter. You know, we have our school, and the people that we've had here at the conservatory, they're coming to the school anyway. So it doesn't matter.
You know. So okay, I received the letter and time went on, and they didn't become national. They decided not to nationalize.

So then he didn't know what to do. So then he writes me a letter, inviting me back. So I said no, man, no. I wouldn't come back if you rode me there in a gold car. I would never come back after you swept me out, you know.
So that's what happened to that job.
: What a shame. What a shame. Too bad.
And the kids. When I went to -- now listen -- when I first went, we had four students, four. When I left we had 89, paying 189 francs -- that's like $40.00 a semester.
Now he decided to junk the jazz program.
So I said, 'Well, if you're that stupid I don't want to work with you anymore.'
